results.title: [2410.17276] Evaluating Performance and Bias of Negative Sampling in Large-Scale Sequential Recommendation Models

item.text: {"text":"Recent work connects fine-grained ranking failures to negative sampling and scoring objectives. [Prakash et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) find that sampling strategies produce different head/mid/tail tradeoffs, which aggregate metrics can conceal. [gSASRec (2024)](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) links sampled BCE training to overconfidence; [Enhanced BPR (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) addresses false negatives that misdirect hard-negative learning. Diagnostic implication: compare positive-versus-candidate score margins within popularity bands and title-similarity bands. These matched comparisons can reveal whether broad semantic relatedness dominates finer distinctions, but do not establish that unobserved candidates are truly unwanted.\n\nRelation type also matters: [TREC’s 2025 recommendation task](https://trec-product-search.github.io/recommendations.html) evaluates substitutes and complements separately, supporting distinctions beyond generic relatedness. For this task, a proposed evidence taxonomy is: explicit textual match, explicit specification conflict, plausible substitute, plausible complement, and unknown. Extract artist, edition, dimensions, connectors, or equipment prerequisites only when titles/descriptions state them; distinguish item-to-item compatibility evidence from unobserved user needs or ownership. Report evidence coverage and unknown rates alongside ranking margins. Missing specifications, absent interactions, and similar titles cannot establish incompatibility, redundancy, rejection, or immediate intent. These probes motivate experiments with mixed uniform/hard sampling, uncertainty-based weighting, and alternative losses; improvements must still be selected using the unchanged macro validation HR@10."}
